catalog_quote: [Kohler, Roberts, Harley & Sena 2025, sec. 1.4.3 'Tone', pp. 66-67:] Like Yoruba, Ife has three discrete level tones (H, M, L) and all vowels as well as surface pre-consonantal and final nasals are tone bearing. The Yoruba M tone has been analysed as underlyingly toneless (Akinlabi 1985; Akinlabi & Liberman 2000: 33-35), but no such analysis has yet been applied to Ife. Kohler (1983: 139, 141) finds no evidence of automatic downstep in Ife, and we confirm that it is absent in HLH forms such as [náàgú ɛ́] ‘in the fufu’. ... indeed Kohler’s Ife dataset contains no contour tones at all. ... in other words, contour tones are prohibited on single moraic tone-bearing units. || [Kohler 1983, p. 139 and p. 141 sec. 2.1, scanned of scan:] Relevons une différence fondamentale sur le plan du ton: le yoruba est une langue à tons à terrasse, tandis que l'ifè est une langue à registres. ... En revanche l'ifé n'a pas d'abaissement. Il semble conserver presque tous les tons, et à leur niveau originel. ... Chaque syllabe ifè porte l'un des trois tons à niveau, soit le bas, le moyen ou le haut.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ifè is described as a three-level-tone language (H, M, L; every vowel and syllabic/surface nasal is a tone-bearing unit; no downstep, no contour tones). None of the accessible descriptions (Kohler et al. 2025 phonological sketch, Gblem-Poidi 2018, Maduagwu & Dare 2016, Peace Corps 2010) says anything about word stress or accent; no stress rule can be extracted.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone described at word level and across word boundaries (V#V processes); stress/accent simply not discussed. Kohler et al. 2025 is a first-hand SIL description based on Kohler's 1980s fieldwork (Atakpamé-area Ifè, Togo) re-checked with a native-speaker co-author.
new_statements.identity_note: Target is Ifè of Togo/Benin (Ana, Ana-Ifè, Baate; ifee1241, ISO ife), an Ede/Yoruboid language — not the Ifẹ̀ dialect of Yoruba spoken at Ilé-Ifẹ̀, Nigeria (Orie 2001 'Ife Yoruba' and Salami 1986 in the Glottolog list concern the Nigerian variety and are mis-tagged). Kohler et al. 2025 rests on Kohler's 1980s SIL fieldwork in the Atakpamé area (Togo) checked by native speaker Komi Sena; Gblem-Poidi 2018 names three variants (Atakpamé town, Dassa/Datcha, Kamina); Klaver 1995 uses the Tchetti dialect (Akparè); Maduagwu & Dare 2016 describe Ifè of Bantè, Benin.

new_statements.quote: La syllabe est composée de phonèmes segmentaux et du ton. Chaque syllabe porte un ton haut (´), moyen (¯) ou bas (`). Une combinaison de deux tons sur une voyelle est interpretée comme une suite de deux syllabes dont la deuxième est une voyelle identique à la voyelle précédente, et avec un ton différent. [p. 112] — Cette étude traite les syllabes et les phonèmes segmentaux du mot grammatical dans sa forme non élidée, c'est-à-dire comme le mot est prononcé en isolation. Le ton sera décrit dans une étude par Anna Kohler dans ce même recueil. [p. 110]
new_statements.translation: The syllable is composed of segmental phonemes and tone. Each syllable carries a high (´), mid (¯) or low (`) tone. A combination of two tones on one vowel is interpreted as a sequence of two syllables whose second is a vowel identical to the preceding vowel, with a different tone. [p. 112] — This study treats the syllables and segmental phonemes of the grammatical word in its unelided form, i.e. as the word is pronounced in isolation. Tone will be described in a study by Anna Kohler in this same volume. [p. 110]

new_statements.relation_note: Same as the existing Kohler et al. 2025 statement: three level tones, all syllables tone-bearing, silent on stress. Adds nothing on stress; describes the Tchetti-canton dialect (speakers from Akparé, Anié, Atakpamé), fieldwork Aug-Sept 1981.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Every syllable (CV, V, or syllabic N) bears one of three level tones H, M, L; no word-level stress or accent is mentioned anywhere in the article (full text searched for accent, stress, proéminence, intensité, emphase: none).
new_statements.exceptions: none on stress; syllable-type note: CVC only in three reduplicated ideophones; two tones on one vowel = two syllables (slightly lengthened vowel with gliding tone)
new_statements.identity_note: Both 1983 works describe the Tchetti/Tchéti (canton) dialect of Ifè in Togo, from three speakers originating in Akparé, Anié and Atakpamé (fieldwork 1981); Boëthius (p. 110) notes there are several Ifè dialects in Togo and that the language is also spoken around Tchetti in Benin. This is the same Togo Ifè as the catalog's Kohler et al. 2025 source (Ife, Togo).

new_statements.quote: Chaque syllabe ifè porte l'un des trois tons à niveau, soit le bas, le moyen ou le haut. Les paires minimales suivantes illustrent cette règle: [p. 141] — Relevons une différence fondamentale sur le plan du ton: le yoruba est une langue à tons à terrasse, tandis que l'ifè est une langue à registres. [...] En revanche l'ifè n'a pas d'abaissement. Il semble conserver presque tous les tons, et à leur niveau originel. Les tons ifè restent donc en principe inchangés. [p. 139]
new_statements.translation: Each Ifè syllable carries one of the three level tones, low, mid or high. The following minimal pairs illustrate this rule: [p. 141] — Note a fundamental difference regarding tone: Yoruba is a terraced-tone language, whereas Ifè is a register-tone language. [...] Ifè, by contrast, has no downstep. It seems to preserve almost all tones, and at their original level. Ifè tones therefore remain in principle unchanged. [p. 139]

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the existing Kohler et al. 2025 statement (three level tones, tone-bearing syllables, silent on stress); the 2025 catalog note's corroborating claim about register tone with no downstep is exactly Kohler 1983 p. 139. Describes the Tchéti dialect (speakers from Akparé, Anié, Atakpamé), fieldwork mid-Aug to mid-Nov 1981.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Three contrastive level tones (H, M, L) on every syllable, a register system without downstep; tone patterns by word class, tone changes (L verbs to M before noun objects; H object pronouns to M after H verbs; utterance-final L realised as low falling), grammatical tone. Word stress or accent is never mentioned (full text searched for accent, stress, proéminence, intensité, emphase: none). The only prominence-like remark, p. 151 sec. 2.2.5(c), is that 'la longueur ou la force du ton haut' of the numeral prefix mé- depends on the numeral's final tone, a tone-realisation observation, not word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: none on stress; tone remarks: only seven of 175 disyllabic nouns have initial H; numerals have irregular prefixation tones; utterance-final L on utterances of 3+ syllables becomes low-falling
new_statements.identity_note: Both 1983 works describe the Tchetti/Tchéti (canton) dialect of Ifè in Togo, from three speakers originating in Akparé, Anié and Atakpamé (fieldwork 1981); Boëthius (p. 110) notes there are several Ifè dialects in Togo and that the language is also spoken around Tchetti in Benin. This is the same Togo Ifè as the catalog's Kohler et al. 2025 source (Ife, Togo).
